title: The Courage to Look Like the Bad Guy
author: Michael Foster
summary: Michael Foster argues that one of the hardest disciplines in parenting, leadership and church life is declining to shield people from the consequences of their own foolishness. He grants that some protection is right, as with a child running into the street, but says lesser consequences are how people learn caution. He draws on a childhood electric fence, a night locked out of the house at sixteen, and parents who regret not being stricter. His claim is that repeated rescue emboldens recklessness and can be one of the most unloving things we do. He extends the principle to letting a child repeat a grade, letting an employee be fired, and the church's practice of excommunication. The closing call is to play the long game and to be willing to look like the bad guy out of love.
points: Shielding someone from every consequence does not protect them; it teaches them that foolishness is free and can embolden them toward recklessness.
The line between a lesson and a catastrophe matters: protect a child from the street, but let the electric fence and the minor failures teach.
A parent who draws a line and keeps it, as Foster's father did when he locked the door, gives a teenager something solid to grow against.
Genuine love sometimes means disappointing people, and the authority figure must accept looking like the bad guy rather than looking the other way.
The same logic explains church discipline: removing someone from the Lord's Table is meant to let the weight of a reckless life lead toward repentance.
quotes: One of the most difficult forms of discipline to practice is choosing not to shield someone from the consequences of their actions.
If you shield people from consequences over and over again, they will continue to act foolishly. It can actually embolden them to become more reckless.
Sometimes one of the most unloving things ever done to someone is shielding him from the consequences of his actions.
My dad drew a line in the sand and maintained it, and that helped me grow up.
There are absolutely times to overlook things. You certainly don’t want to make things bigger than they are, and there’s a big difference between simple mistakes and deliberate foolishness.
We must cultivate a gracious attitude that loves people enough to disappoint them, even when that means letting them take a hard landing without cushioning the fall.

Whether it’s letting your child repeat a grade, letting someone get fired from a job, or excommunicating an unrepentant church member, you must have the courage to look like the bad guy and not look the other way.
